column1: What two axes does standard music notation map pitch and time onto?
column2: Vertical position on the staff = pitch (frequency); horizontal position = time.

column1: What note does the treble clef (G-clef) anchor, and where?
column2: G4 — the clef's spiral center curls around the 2nd line from the bottom of the staff.

column1: What note does the bass clef (F-clef) anchor, and where?
column2: F3 — the two dots of the clef straddle the 4th line from the bottom of the staff.

column1: Where does Middle C (C4) sit relative to the treble and bass staves?
column2: On a ledger line: the 1st ledger line below the treble staff, which is the same pitch as the 1st ledger line above the bass staff — the hinge connecting both hands on the grand staff.

column1: Why is 'letter-counting' from a known note considered a beginner mistake in sight-reading?
column2: It's too slow for performance tempo; trained readers recognize staff positions as shapes/intervals relative to memorized anchor notes, not by counting line-space-line-space.

column1: What do the treble clef space names spell, bottom to top?
What mnemonic is used for the treble clef line names bottom to top, and what are they?
column2: "Good Boys Do Fine Always" — E4, G4, B4, D5, F5.

column1: What is the core rule for how beaming eighth notes conveys metric information?
column2: Beams show subdivision structure, not decoration: in 4/4 eighths beam in groups of 2 (marking the beat); in 6/8 they beam in groups of 3 (marking the compound beat). Oddly-beamed notes signal an irregular beat structure.

column1: What is the practical rule for choosing a clef for an instrument's part?
column2: Choose the clef that centers the instrument's working range on the staff with the fewest ledger lines, since ledger lines are where sight-reading errors occur (e.g., cello switches to tenor clef in high/thumb position to avoid 4+ ledger lines above bass clef).

column1: What does transposing a melody up a perfect fifth mean spatially on the staff, and what else must be adjusted?
column2: Shift every notehead up 4 staff positions and adjust the key signature accordingly — it's a spatial/fingering shift, not a frequency calculation.

column1: What is the relationship between keys a fifth apart on the circle of fifths?
column2: They differ by exactly one accidental (e.g., C major has none, G major has one sharp, F major has one flat) — this is the mechanical backbone of modulation and transposition.

column1: What is the single governing rule for whether a notation choice is 'correct' according to the Advanced Notational Techniques lesson?
column2: A trained performer must be able to look at the symbol once and know exactly what to do with their hands, at tempo, without re-reading it; if it forces a second look, simplify it or add a legend.
